newsitem.title: SPAIN: Gonzalez stuns Spanish Socialists with resignation.
newsitem.headline: Gonzalez stuns Spanish Socialists with resignation.

text.p: Former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who led Spain for 13 years, stunned supporters on Friday by announcing he would not seek reelection as Socialist party chief.

"I will continue to be available to serve this party but you should now hear that it will not be as secretary general of the party," he told more than a thousand delegates at the 34th Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) Congress in Madrid.
The surprise move, which caught even party faithful off guard, is seen as a bold but necessary step toward revitalising the Socialist movement in Spain.
"It's very risky, but it can pave the way for the future," Joaquin Leguina, a leading party member, told journalists.
Gonzalez's reelection as PSOE leader had been seen as a mere formality at a three-day party congress which opened on Friday. All that changed when he took the stage for his opening speech.

With Gonzalez as its leader the party became almost synonymous with democracy in Spain, steering the country through rapid economic and social change in the 1980s after nearly 40 years of fascist dictatorship.

But the glory days came to an end early this decade as corruption scandals repeatedly surfaced and top officials were accused of having run a "dirty war" from 1983 to 1987 against Basque separatist rebels.
By 1993, the party was limping badly and scraped through to victory in a general election mainly because of lingering fears that the right-wing opposition would return to dictatorship.

When the Socialists were finally knocked from power last May by the conservative Popular Party led by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, their party leadership was directionless and in desperate need of an overhaul.
But there was no other leader with enough popular support to step forward and pull the Socialists together.

Politicial analysts had predicted that Gonzalez, still Spain's most popular politician, would use the congress to clear out dead wood on the party executive and make room for someone to eventually replace him.
Gonzalez has frequently spoken of being tired of public life and has pushed his party to renew itself.
In his speech he talked about the need for "a change of generations" and referred to the new, young leaders who have returned Socialist parties to power in Britain and in France.

In the run-up to the congress, Alfonso Guerra, number two in the party and a fierce Socialist traditionalist, had made it clear he would not quit voluntarily but followed Gonzalez on Friday by stepping down.

Guerra, who grew up with Gonzalez and fought alongside him through years of exile, is critical of the more centrist attitude of the modern Socialist party and had threatened to split the party, pulling his left-wing followers with him.
Party barons said Gonzalez's radical move had left them breathless, but they recognised it as necessary to take back the initiative from Guerra.

The 55-year-old Gonzalez gave no clear signal who he wanted to succeed him and his gesture opened the way for a leadership battle to determine who will carry the Socialist banner into the next general election, scheduled for the year 2000.
There are no obvious candidates and delegates were shaking their heads in amazement at the job ahead of them. "Look at huge task you have left us," party spokesman Luis Yanez told Gonzalez.
Delegates mentioned NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister, and Barcelona mayor Pasqual Maragall as potential candidates.
Others speculated that Gonzalez himself could be coaxed into changing his mind and standing for reelection.

"Everyone thought it could happen but we never thought he would really do it," said Felix Dillana, a delegate from the Extremadura region. "You could see on the faces of the executive committee that even they didn't know it was coming."
Gonzalez asked for respect and consideration for what he had done and left the stage to a standing ovation.
"He made a great gesture for democracy and for Spain," Socialist parliamentary president Joaquin Almunia said. "I think he has shown his generosity with this party."
